Senses.Explanation: The wet-footed slog of the teaching life, praised, diagnosed, and owned as the price of staying down among people. Yuanwu Keqin splits the two stances: eyes on the Milky Way with no favor to human feeling, or ash-headed and mud-faced dragging water and mud — then folds them: thus-in-not-thus levels the heights, not-thus-in-thus lets go from empty space; Baiyu Jingsi, in the long rain with the stove bare and the grain gone, has Samantabhadra dragging water and mud while Manjusri sighs silently, and the hall's silent sage can only applaud the donor's snow-day charcoal; Yinyuan Longqi, leaving Huangbo after eight hard years of scolding wind and rain, verses the send-off — today I go dragging water and mud, and the twelve peaks break into smiles; and Shiqi Tongyun, closing the summer, grants the hut on the lonely peak to the hut-builder and free play at the crossroads to the player — cliff-standing and mud-dragging are all within one's lot. Baichi Xingyuan, hearing that some nose-less ones sneer behind his back that Baishan loves granny-talk, owns the slander: snatching plow and grain is idle matter — dragging water and mud gets harder and harder to watch; Sanshan Denglai, at his opening furnace, rules that question traded for question drags water and mud and raised fist and finger add nails and wedges; Baochi Xuanzong promises the step that knows high and low at first tread: it spares Sakra a fright, spares the carp its beating, frees one from dragging water and mud and from searching the road; and Tianyin Yuanxiu, leaving the mountain that took fifteen years to build, verses the departure — repaying grace has nothing to do with it, now I too go dragging water and mud, staff and hat in the wind over far mountains.

Senses.Explanation: Burning the crown of the head is literal bodily burning offered as devotion, recompense, or proof of serious intent. These distinct uses keep the act literal without claiming that every passage records the same ceremony.

Senses.Note: Guishan gives the line when Xiangyan asks him to explain what he himself cannot say, and again in the records of Dongshan’s inquiry. Guishan’s refusal does not end the encounter; it makes the student meet the issue directly. Senses.Explanation: Dahui and Taiyuan Fu use one's inborn nostrils for what is already one's own and need not be sought elsewhere or forced into shape. Dahui says that after the dog-case breaks open, one knows that the nostrils received from one's parents have been on one's face all along. In the Blue Cliff Record, Fu announces after awakening that he will no longer twist those nostrils. The body part remains literal in both sayings; its obvious location and natural shape do the work.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records turn the time before one’s birth into a pointed interview location from which a person’s original face, identity, or decisive word is demanded. Xueyan Zuqin asks what it ultimately is before one’s parents gave birth. An identified lay questioner surnamed Wan turns his surname into a challenge about what he was called before that time. A verse attributed to Huineng answers with ‘originally not a single thing,’ while Tianyin Yuanxiu reports the phrase as a question repeatedly assigned for investigation. Other records keep the answers concrete and discordant: an unnamed monastic asks for the original face, Yushan Shangsi pairs before-birth with a stone mortar fried in oil and after-birth with a steelyard weight dipped in snow, and Zhe’an Jingfan says that recognizing the person in a crowd also reveals this original face. These witnesses support the recurring temporal challenge without promoting any one answer into its definition.

Senses.Explanation: The clause asks about the time before one's parents were born; the seven exact witnesses use it as a teaching contrast, a question, a measure of what is already complete, and a formulation of the face to be seen. Yuanwu Keqin sets 'before father and mother were born' (父母未生已前) against 'after father and mother were born' and the completed body. Gulin Qingmao says that before one's parents were born there was already a line for repaying beneficence (父母未生已前，便有報德酧恩一句). Taiyuan Fu asks Gushan where the nostrils were before one's parents were born (父母未生已前，鼻孔在什麼處). Chushi Fanqi asks how the time before one's parents were born compares with the current occasion (父母未生已前，何似這個時節). Cijue Puyin asks a respondent where he traveled before his parents were born and strikes him as he prepares to answer (父母未生已前，在甚麼處行履). Yinyuan Longqi says that, as for recommendation, it was already finished before one's parents were born (父母未生已前薦拔已竟). Konggu Daocheng links seeing the faces of the buddhas to seeing the face before one's parents were born (父母未生已前面目). The corpus thus bends the temporal clause into a recurring interview boundary and face-formulation; these witnesses do not supply one uniform answer.

Senses.Note: The classical line says that father and son conceal for one another. Fushi reads Xinghua’s severe treatment of Kebin through that mutual bond. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1386.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shitian Faxun. Shitian Faxun raises Wuzu's poem: golden chrysanthemums grow from old roots in the courtyard, one or two returning geese are heard, and seven peaks stirred last night's interest into thinking until dawn. Shitian says Wuzu's verbal path is clear but few know his heart. He then announces a different turn at Fengqiao, repeats the courtyard and geese, and replaces Wuzu's last two lines with the gold-whip and night-street pair. The headword is Shitian's rewritten ending, not the unchanged earlier poem. It turns solitary thought about the peaks into an addressed returning traveler and a question about someone to walk with. No listener answers and no actual journey or use of the whip is narrated; the altered ending invites the assembly to meet the poem's challenge rather than merely admire its clarity.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua. Ying'an Tanhua raises Danxia visiting the sleeping national teacher. The attendant says the teacher is present but sees no guests, and adds that even a Buddha's eye cannot see him. Danxia praises dragon and phoenix offspring. Hearing the account after waking, the national teacher strikes the attendant twenty times and drives him out; Danxia says he is rightly called the national teacher. Ying'an calls the attendant's beating and departure a rare event, admits his own eagerness at it, and says that even skillful Danxia falls into the teacher's net. Can the listeners distinguish this? If not, he gives the gold-whip pair. The headword is Ying'an's current appeal after the old actions, not the attendant's speech or a new whip beating. The praise, punishment and net are deliberately left in tension rather than reduced to a simple verdict that the attendant failed.

Invited to give a short instruction at Chengtian, Wuchu Daguan first describes guests and host harmonizing like a lid fitting its box, with a clay ox roaring at the moon and a wooden horse neighing in the wind. That is all very well, but what if someone brings out the weapons of the three mysteries and fixes the positions of ruler and ministers? How could that be met? He strikes his whisk and gives the gold-whip and night-street pair. The question breaks into the opening harmony instead of certifying it as complete. The couplet is Wuchu's present response to his own proposed test; the source does not report a visitor actually producing weapons or an assembly member accepting a night walk.
